diagnosis_plain: Feline CKD IRIS Stage 2–3, mild systemic hypertension, borderline proteinuria

pet.chief_complaint: Progressive weight loss over 12 months; increased water intake; abnormal kidney values on routine annual bloodwork
pet.report_type: Serum biochemistry panel, CBC, SDMA, blood pressure, urinalysis + UPC ratio
pet.history: No prior known illness; gradual weight loss over 12 months; increased water intake noted in past 1–2 months

summary.severity: Significant — IRIS Stage 2–3 CKD with three progression accelerators: elevated phosphorus, hypertension, borderline proteinuria
summary.findings_count: 6 key parameters reviewed (creatinine, BUN, SDMA, phosphorus, blood pressure, UPC)
summary.decision_window: Intervene now — Whiskey is currently compensated; acting before decompensation gives the best quality-of-life outcomes
summary.prognosis: Good with active management; IRIS Stage 2 median survival ~3–4 years; phosphorus control and BP management are the highest-impact interventions
summary.paths: 5 interventions ranked by priority: renal diet · phosphate binder · amlodipine · subQ fluids · telmisartan
summary.priority_match: Staged approach — renal diet + amlodipine now; reassess phosphate binder and subQ fluids at 4–6 week recheck
summary.next_step: Start renal wet food transition and amlodipine immediately; recheck BP + BMP + UPC in 4–6 weeks

findings.name: Creatinine
findings.meaning: Above normal — confirms reduced glomerular filtration rate; places Whiskey at IRIS Stage 2–3 boundary

findings.name: BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen)
findings.meaning: Elevated — reduced clearance of protein metabolic waste; supports CKD diagnosis alongside creatinine

findings.name: SDMA
findings.meaning: Early-sensitive kidney biomarker — elevation reflects ~40–50% nephron loss; confirms CKD even when creatinine is borderline

findings.name: Phosphorus
findings.meaning: Borderline elevated — phosphorus retention in CKD directly accelerates nephron loss; dietary management is high priority

findings.name: Blood Pressure
findings.meaning: Mildly hypertensive — damages remaining nephrons and significantly increases risk of retinal detachment (acute blindness)

findings.name: UPC (Urine Protein:Creatinine Ratio)
findings.meaning: Borderline proteinuric — persistent protein loss through damaged filtration membranes accelerates tubular injury and CKD progression

paths.label: Option A
paths.survival: Strong evidence: extends median survival 2–3× in IRIS Stage 2–3 compared to regular food; single highest-impact intervention
paths.aligns: Non-invasive; wet food simultaneously provides hydration; phosphorus restriction addresses two problems at once; immediately actionable
paths.tensions: Some cats resist new foods — transition must be gradual (2–4 weeks); switching too fast risks food aversion; protein restriction must be balanced to avoid muscle wasting

paths.label: Option B
paths.survival: Strong when serum phosphorus remains >4.5 mg/dL after diet transition; directly reduces phosphorus-driven nephron loss
paths.aligns: Powder or liquid mixed with food; minimal handling stress; essential if phosphorus does not normalize on renal diet alone
paths.tensions: Not necessary if renal diet alone normalizes phosphorus — reassess at 4–6 week recheck before starting; different binders suit different cats

paths.label: Option C
paths.survival: Strong evidence: first-line antihypertensive in cats; essential at BP >160 mmHg; prevents retinal detachment, stroke, and nephron loss
paths.aligns: Small daily dose (compounded liquid or 1/8 tablet); low-stress administration; rapid BP reduction typically seen within 1–2 weeks
paths.tensions: Initial BP recheck in 7–10 days needed to confirm dose adequacy; some cats need dose adjustment; white-coat hypertension possible — consider baseline home BP monitoring

paths.label: Option D
paths.survival: Moderate evidence: improves well-being and reduces azotemia in dehydrated cats; most beneficial at IRIS Stage 3+
paths.aligns: Corrects subclinical dehydration that kidneys can no longer compensate; many owners successfully learn the technique; can be done every 2–3 days
paths.tensions: Requires in-clinic training; some cats resist restraint; at Stage 2 with good hydration, not yet urgent — revisit at next recheck

paths.label: Option E
paths.survival: Moderate: telmisartan reduces UPC in cats; benazepril has less feline-specific evidence; most beneficial when UPC ≥0.4
paths.aligns: Targets proteinuria directly; secondary nephroprotective effect; can be compounded into palatable liquid form
paths.tensions: At UPC 0.3, intervention threshold is borderline — recheck UPC in 4–6 weeks; if rising, strong indication to start; avoid ACE inhibitors if severely dehydrated

prognosis_bullets: IRIS Stage 2 CKD with active management: median survival approximately 1,150–1,500 days (~3–4 years) from diagnosis
IRIS Stage 3 CKD with active management: median survival ~250–350 days from diagnosis; outcomes vary greatly based on BP and phosphorus control
Renal diet is the single strongest prognostic intervention: phosphorus restriction reduces progression by 2–3× compared to regular food
Uncontrolled hypertension (BP >180 mmHg): significantly increases risk of acute onset blindness from retinal detachment — a preventable emergency
Proteinuria monitoring is critical: UPC >0.4 is associated with ~3× faster CKD progression rate; track at every recheck
prognosis_note: Whiskey's current status is encouraging for a 14-year-old cat with CKD — he is compensated, eating, and interactive. The goal is not to cure CKD but to slow it substantially. With a renal diet, blood pressure control, and phosphorus management, cats at his stage commonly maintain excellent quality of life for 2–3+ years. A staged, measured approach is both medically sound and less stressful for him.
questions: Based on the full panel, are we at IRIS Stage 2 or Stage 3? This determines whether subcutaneous fluids are a priority now or can wait.
Should we recheck blood pressure at a calm, low-stress visit before starting amlodipine, or is 168 mmHg reliably above the treatment threshold?
Which renal diet do you recommend — wet food (preferred for hydration) or dry? Can I transition Whiskey gradually by mixing with his current food?
If phosphorus is still above 4.5 mg/dL after 4–6 weeks on the renal diet, which phosphate binder do you recommend and how is it administered?
Whiskey's UPC is 0.3 — at what level would you recommend starting telmisartan, and when should we recheck the UPC?
Should Whiskey have a fundic eye exam now to check for early hypertensive retinopathy, given his blood pressure?
What signs should prompt an urgent vet visit versus monitoring at home — is it vomiting, complete appetite loss, sudden hiding, or something else?
